lesson.title: Solving the Impossible Handshake: How Strangers Share a Secret
lesson.summary: Public key, or asymmetric, cryptography gives every party a mathematically linked pair of keys, a public one anyone can see and a private one only they hold, which finally solves the key distribution problem that symmetric encryption alone cannot.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter ended on a genuine problem: two parties with no shared secret and no already secure channel cannot use symmetric encryption to safely exchange a key, because sending the key itself would require the very security they are trying to establish in the first place. Public key cryptography, also called asymmetric cryptography, escapes this by giving each party not one key but a mathematically related pair: a public key that can be shared with absolutely anyone, including adversaries, and a private key that is never shared with anyone at all.

The reason this works comes down to what mathematicians call a trapdoor function, a calculation that is easy to perform in one direction but computationally infeasible to reverse without a piece of extra information, the trapdoor, that only the key's owner has. RSA, one well known public key system, builds its trapdoor around the difficulty of factoring the product of two very large prime numbers. Multiplying two large primes together is fast. Starting only from that product and working backward to recover the two original primes is, for sufficiently large numbers, prohibitively slow even for powerful computers, unless you already know one of the factors. That asymmetry between easy forward and hard backward is what lets a public key be safely published while its matching private key stays secret.

Here is a concrete example of how this solves Alice and Bob's problem. Bob generates a key pair and publishes his public key openly, perhaps on his website, where anyone, including an eavesdropper, can see it. Alice wants to send Bob a secret message. She takes Bob's public key and uses it to encrypt her message. She sends the resulting ciphertext to Bob, over a network an attacker might be watching the entire time. That attacker sees the ciphertext and also already knows Bob's public key, since it was never secret, but neither of those things helps them, because only Bob's private key can decrypt something that was encrypted with his matching public key. Alice and Bob never had to meet, never had to whisper a secret over a trusted line, and never had to solve the circular problem that stumped symmetric encryption alone. A closely related idea, used heavily in real protocols like SSH and TLS, is a key agreement scheme such as Diffie-Hellman: instead of Alice encrypting a message to Bob, both sides generate their own private value, exchange public values derived from those private values, and each independently combines their own private value with the other side's public value to land on the exact same shared secret, one that an eavesdropper watching every public value cross the network still cannot reconstruct.

Given that public key cryptography solves the key distribution problem so elegantly, it is worth asking why symmetric encryption is not simply retired. The answer is speed. The mathematical operations behind RSA or elliptic curve cryptography are dramatically more computationally expensive than the simple block operations behind AES, often by a factor of a hundred or more for equivalent amounts of data. Using pure asymmetric encryption to protect an entire video stream or file transfer would be far slower than it needs to be. Real protocols exploit the strengths of both instead of choosing one: use the slower asymmetric cryptography just once, briefly, at the start of a connection, purely to agree on a fresh symmetric key, and then switch to fast symmetric encryption for the actual data that follows. This hybrid pattern is exactly what SSH does under the hood, and it is the central design decision behind TLS, covered in detail later in this unit.
